reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Hailey sat in the cafe with Mom. Mom gave her a pencil and a paper menu. "Can you write your name?" Mom asked. Hailey wanted to write it so much. She grabbed the pencil in her whole fist. She pushed hard. The letters came out wiggly and ugly. The H looked like a squished bug.

Mom took Hailey's little hand. She set the pencil on Hailey's middle finger. Then Mom helped her pinch the top with her thumb and one finger. "Try now," Mom said softly. Hailey pinched and squeezed. The pencil felt steady, like a paint brush in her hand.

She drew one line down. Then another line down. Then a line across. It was an H! Hailey laughed. "The pencil stays still when I pinch it," she said. She drew a big A next. The waitress came by and clapped. Mom gave the paper a kiss and put it in her bag. "The best H I ever saw," said Mom. Hailey pinched the pencil again and wrote one more A.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Lily sat in the computer lab at school. In front of her was a tablet. It was dark and still. She wanted to draw a cat on it. But first she had to turn it on.

Lily found the small round button on the side. She pushed it. She waited. She counted, "One, two, three." Then the screen lit up. "The button makes it turn on!" said Lily. On the screen was a row of little pictures. One, two, three, four, five. She looked for the drawing app.

She tapped the picture with the crayon. The app opened. Lily drew a purple cat with a straight tail. She drew one ear, two ears, three whiskers. Then the teacher said it was time to go.

Lily moved her finger across the screen. The cat was gone. She pressed the button again and held it. "One, two, three." The screen went dark. She put the tablet back on the shelf, straight in a line with the others.

"I pressed it, and it slept," said Lily.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story: Sarah went to the store with Mom. She wanted apples for snack. But how many apples should they get? Mom did not say. "Can you count them?" asked Mom. Sarah held up her hands. She did not guess. She knew the counting song. "One, two, three," she said, touching each apple. "Four, five, six, seven." The apples were red and round. One apple had a triangle sticker on it. "That sticker is cute," said Sarah. She kept going. "Eight, nine, ten." The words came out in the same order as her song. Ten came last, every time. "Did I count right?" she asked. "Yes! Ten apples," said Mom. "Ten apples because the song goes one to ten, and then it stops." Mom put the apples in a bag. The bag went in the cart. Sarah held the bag all the way to the car. "One bag," she said. "Ten apples."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Ibrahim sat in his big car seat. They were going to Grandpa's house. The sun came up early, and the road was bright.

Ibrahim dropped his toy car. It fell under the seat. He could not reach it. "Mama, can you help me, please?" he asked. Mama reached back and got it. "Thank you, Mama," said Ibrahim. She smiled at him in the mirror.

Then they stopped for apples. Papa gave one to Ibrahim. But Ibrahim squeezed it too hard, and it rolled onto Mama's lap. "Sorry, Mama," he said. Mama wiped her dress. "That is okay," she said. Then they crossed a big bridge. Water ran under it. "That is a river," said Ibrahim. "Can we pass it soon?" Papa drove on and on.

After the bridge, Mama gave Ibrahim his apple again. It tasted sweet. "The apple rolled because I held it too hard," said Ibrahim. He held it soft this time. "Good hands," said Mama. Ibrahim took a big, happy bite.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Lydia stood on the grass by the baseball diamond. She had a purple beanbag and a big red ball. Papa put a hoop on the ground.

"Throw the beanbag in," said Papa.

Lydia threw it. The beanbag went far left. It landed in the grass.

"Not yet," said Lydia.

She brought the beanbag back. She looked at the hoop. She threw again, slow and soft. This time the beanbag dropped in.

"Slow and soft," said Lydia. "It goes in when I throw soft."

Papa clapped. Then he picked up the big red ball.

"Now catch," he said. "Hold out both hands."

Lydia held out one hand. Papa rolled the ball. It bumped her hand and rolled away.

"Not yet," said Lydia.

She brought the ball back. This time she held out both hands. She made a big bowl with them. Papa rolled the ball again. It rolled right into her hands.

"Both hands catch the ball!" said Lydia.

"Both hands," said Papa. "Big ball, big hands."

They sat on the bench. Papa gave Lydia a purple card with a star on it.

"You get a star," said Papa.

Lydia held the card up high. "My star," she said. "My big hands, too."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Charlie wanted to wear her bear pajamas to bed. But she could not find them anywhere.

"Where did they go?" she asked. "Did they run away?"

"No," said Dad with a smile. "Look in the laundry basket."

There they were. The pajamas were wet. Charlie had splashed in her bath, and now the pajamas had fallen in the puddle on the floor. "Wet pajamas got wet because of my bath water," said Charlie. "That is why!"

Dad laughed. "You are a smart detective."

They hung the pajamas on the radiator. Dad said they would be dry by morning, because warm air dries wet things. Charlie put on her bunny pajamas instead. They were soft and warm.

Before bed, Charlie ate a banana and brushed her teeth. Dad tucked her in.

"Will my bear pajamas be dry for school?" Charlie asked.

"Yes, after the warm air bakes them dry all night," said Dad.

Charlie hugged her bunny pajamas. "Good night, bunnies. The radiator is baking my bears."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Addison went to the library with her dad. She wanted to build with the big blocks. The blocks sat in a red bin.

She stacked a square block on top. It sat still. Then she tried to stack a circle block. The circle rolled away. It rolled under the chair. "Come back!" said Addison. She got on her knees. She reached under the chair. Her dad laughed. "That circle is fast," he said.

Addison put the circle on the rug. She pushed it. It rolled again. She put a square on the rug. She pushed it. The square just slid. It did not roll. She scratched her head. "The circle rolls because it is round," she said. "The square has flat sides. Flat sides stop it."

She stacked squares and triangles and rectangles. They all sat still. At the top she put one circle. It wobbled. It rolled off and bonked her toe. "Ow! Silly circle," she said. Her dad kissed her toe. Then he read her a story about a mean dragon who could not roll down a hill. "He is too square," said Addison. Her dad laughed and laughed. She pushed the circle one more time, and it rolled all the way to the story door.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
James wanted to paint a big green tree. The teacher let him pick a paint pot. But the green pot was frozen. It had been outside in the cold all night. James tapped the pot. The paint would not move. "We can let it warm up," said Miss Kim. James waited. He looked out the window. The tree was still green. The pot was still hard.

Then James saw the blue pot. He saw the yellow pot too. He put blue on his brush. He put yellow on top. He stirred them on the paper. The paint turned green! "Blue and yellow make green," said James. "That is the name of my new color. Tree green." Miss Kim smiled. James painted his tree, slow and careful, from the brown pot to the green leaves. "Look at my tree," he said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Athena stood in the kitchen with her family. She wanted to help make breakfast.

Daddy poured big pancakes. Athena poured one small pancake. "Mine is small like a coin," she said. The pan was hot, so the pancakes sizzled fast. Athena wanted her small pancake to be a magic cake for the moon.

But the small pancake cooked fast. The big pancakes cooked slow. Athena watched her coin pancake. It turned brown quickly. "Oh no!" she cried. Her magic cake was too dark.

Daddy smiled. "Small things cook fast," he said. "Big things cook slow." Athena thought about this. Then she made a new plan. She made a big pancake, as big as a plate. It cooked slowly, slowly. It stayed golden and perfect.

Athena put the big pancake on a cold plate from the fridge. The plate felt cold on her fingers. "Moon cake!" she said. Her curly hair bounced as she jumped. Daddy took a bite. "Best moon cake ever," he said. Athena giggled and poured more batter.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Beatrice loved the doll corner at school. Today she found three baby dolls in the basket. One baby, two babies, three babies. She picked up the smallest one.

"You are crying," said Beatrice. The baby was really just quiet plastic. But her friend Milo sat nearby. He was the daddy in their pretend house. "The baby is hungry," said Milo. Beatrice looked around. There was no real food.

Then she had an idea. She took a small red block. She held it like a bottle. "Here, baby, here is your milk." She tipped the block to the baby's mouth. She made a tiny slurp sound, "slurp, slurp, slurp." Milo clapped his hands. The baby was all better now.

"She stopped crying because I fed her," said Beatrice. "Hungry babies cry. Full babies sleep." She laid the baby on a scarf for a blanket. She had to bend down low to tuck it in. She patted the baby's back, one pat, two pats, three pats.

Then Milo brought a toy phone. "Ring, ring! The doctor is here!" Beatrice grabbed it. "Hello, Doctor Beatrice speaking." The baby needed one more check-up. She pressed a finger on the baby's chest. "Beep! All healthy!" Milo laughed so big.

At tidy-up time, Beatrice put the babies back in the basket. One baby, two babies, three babies. She was happy. "Same game tomorrow?" asked Milo. Beatrice nodded. "Bring the phone," she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Milo ran to the bunny cage. He wanted to hold Snowy today.

"Snowy had a turn yesterday," said Miss Kim. She was a kind woman with a soft voice. "Amy held him yesterday. Today is Tom's turn. Tomorrow you can hold him."

Milo frowned. He did not want tomorrow. He wanted now.

"It is not tomorrow now," said Tom. Tom held Snowy gently.

Milo waited. He fixed his loose shoe lace. He drew a bunny. He paid careful attention when Miss Kim read a story. The story was long.

The bell rang. Mom came to get Milo.

"Did you hold the bunny?" Mom asked.

"Not yet," said Milo. "I get my turn tomorrow."

He slept. Then the sun came up. Milo put on his shoes fast.

"Is it tomorrow now?" he asked Mom.

Mom smiled. "Yes. Now eat your breakfast."

At school, Milo held Snowy. Snowy was warm and soft.

"Tomorrow turned into today," said Milo.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
story:
Lillian had a cold. She caught it from her big brother. Now she had to stay home.

Lillian wanted to play. She picked up her toy plane. She ran down the hall. But her nose was stuffy. Her legs felt slow. She sat on the floor and sighed.

Mom made her a warm drink. Mom tucked her into bed with her plane. Lillian slept and slept. When she woke up, her nose was better. Her legs felt fast again.

Lillian ran to Mom. "Mom, my cold is almost gone!" she said. She held up her plane. "I slept, and now I feel good."

Mom smiled. "Yes, my sweet girl."

Lillian threw the plane across the room. It flew in a big loop. She ran and caught it. Her nose did not run anymore. She laughed and threw it again.

"Again!" said Lillian. "Watch me catch it!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
James went to the bank with Mom. Outside it was cold and windy. James did not want to be cold.

"Time for your coat," said Mom. "I can do it," said James. He pushed his arms in. One arm went in fast. The other arm hid. He wiggled and wiggled. At last the arm popped out. The coat was on!

Now came the zipper. James pulled it up. But it would not zip. It just slid and slid. Why would it not go? James looked down. The zipper had two sides. One side was up high. One side was down low. They were not together.

James touched the little slider at the bottom. What if the two sides had to meet there first? He pushed both sides down. He pushed them into the slider. Click. He pulled the zipper up. Zip! It went all the way to his chin. "The two parts touch at the bottom," said James. "Then it zips!"

Mom smiled. "What a good zipper job," she said. James saw a picture on the wall. It had a snowman in a coat. "His coat zips too," said James. He patted his own chest and walked out the door.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Mohamed went to the market with Dad. He held a big red bag. "We need eggs," said Dad. "We need milk," said Mohamed. "Pancakes for dinner tonight!"

A fly buzzed near the apples. It did a little loop. "Silly fly," laughed Mohamed. "No pancakes for you."

At home, Mohamed helped cook. Dad let him stir. The batter was lumpy. Mohamed stirred more. The lumps went away because he stirred. "Look, Dad! Smooth now!"

Then Dad tapped the shelf. A hook was loose. He got his hammer. Tap, tap, tap. "All fixed," said Dad. "Now the pan can hang."

Mohamed poured batter into the hot pan. It sizzled. It smelled sweet and warm. Dad flipped one pancake high. It flew up, up, up. Then it landed right in the pan.

"Again!" laughed Mohamed.

The pancakes stacked up on a big plate. Mama and Baby Amina came to the table. Mohamed gave everyone two pancakes. He ate his bite and grinned.

"Best pancakes ever," said Mama.

Mohamed licked syrup off his thumb. "Tomorrow we flip three!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Rosalie rode in the car a long, long way. "We are far from home," she said. Her feet felt the warm sand. "This beach is not cold like winter," she said. Winter at home made her wear boots. Here she wore tiny flip flops.

Rosalie found a tiny white shell. She put it in her pocket. Then she splashed in the sea. Her swimsuit got all wet. She sat down on the hot sand. The sun shone and shone. Soon her swimsuit was dry!

"Why is it dry?" she wondered. The sun did it. The wet went away because the sun was hot. She asked, "Did the sun drink my water?"

Then Mama's phone made a sound. It was Grandma! Rosalie got to call out, "Hello, Grandma! The sun dried my suit!" The waves said swoosh, swoosh.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
story:
Kai was at Grandma's house. Grandma had a gift for him. It was a little red drum. In the corner, gold fish did swim in a bowl. Grandma turned on a song.

Kai clapped. His claps were too fast. The drum went boom, boom, boom. "Too fast," said Grandma. She clapped slow and steady, like a big clock. Tick, tock, tick, tock. Kai watched. Then he tried. He clapped when Grandma clapped. Now his claps fit the song.

Then Grandma sang, "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." She sang it slow. Kai listened. He sang the next words by himself. He did not forget them. "How I wonder what you are," he sang, and clapped on each beat. The naughty cat jumped up and tapped the drum with her paw. Boom. "The cat can clap too!" said Kai.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Jaxon stayed at Grandma's house. He wanted to wear his dinosaur socks. Grandma said, "Bath time first." Jaxon was shy about the big tub. He knocked on the side with his knuckles. It sounded like a drum. Then he climbed in. The warm water made him smile. He made a line of bubbles along his arm, all the way to his elbow.

After the bath, Grandma gave him a soft towel. She hung the wet towel on the line outside the window. Then Jaxon tried to put on his dinosaur socks. They stuck on his toes. He pulled and pulled. The socks would not go on. "My feet are still wet," Jaxon said. "Wet feet make socks stick." Grandma smiled. "Dry them first," she said.

She patted his toes with the towel until they were dry and warm. The socks slid right on. Jaxon looked down at the dinosaurs. They looked like they were dancing on his feet. Grandma handed him his cup of milk. "Socks on fast now," said Jaxon. "Because my feet are dry." He took a big sip and wiggled his toes.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Jake went to the library with his mom. Story time was about bees. Jake wanted the big bee puppet more than anything. He reached for it fast.

But a girl named Mia had it first. She hugged the bee and made it buzz. Jake froze. His hand stopped in the air. Then he said, "Can I have a turn next?" Mia nodded and kept buzzing. After one song, she held out the bee. "Your turn," she said.

Jake made the bee fly to the moon. Then a boy asked, "My turn?" Jake passed the bee right over. The teacher clapped. "We all share, so we all get turns," she said. At the end, the library got messy with pillows everywhere. Jake helped stack them in a tall tower. "Goodbye, bee," he whispered, and the bee seemed to wink.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
story:
Isla went to the pharmacy with Dad. There was a little sink by the counter. Isla wanted a snack from her bag. "First, hands," said Dad.

Isla turned on the water. She put soap on her hands. She rubbed and rubbed. It was hard to know when to stop. Then a song came from a toy fox on the shelf. Isla began to sing along. She washed her hands the whole song. "All clean!" she said.

The pharmacist smiled and gave her a sticker. It was a little fox with bubbles. Later, Isla used the toilet. She ran back and sang her song again while she washed. Then she ate her snack. The crackers tasted good. "Clean hands," said Isla, holding up her sticker.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Eli sat on his bed. He had a new book from the library. It had a red cover and a picture of a frog. On the back was a big pot. The frog wanted to jump into the pot.

Eli opened the book. He saw little marks on the page. "Those are words," he said. The words sat under the pictures. His mom read them out loud. The marks told what the frog did. First the frog hops. Then the frog jumps into the pot. The words said so. The pictures did not say it. The words did.

Eli turned the pages one by one. He started at the front. He went to the back. The last page showed the frog sleeping. Eli patted the cover. "My book," he said. He put it under his pillow.

The next morning, Mom held out a bag. "We take the book back today," she said. Eli shook his head. He held the book tight. At the library, a girl stood by the desk. She was waiting. She pointed at the red cover. "I want the frog book next," she said. Eli looked at her. He looked at his book. He gave it to the librarian. She put a card in it. "You can borrow it again," she said. Eli jumped once, soft, on the library floor. The girl sat down with the book. She opened the front page first.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
Eleanor woke up on her birthday. She was four today! Mom said, "Your cake has four candles now. You are one year older, so we add one candle."

Grandma and Grandpa came. Ben from next door came too. Everyone sang the birthday song. Eleanor clapped her hands.

Then the candles. Four little flames stood on the cake. "Make a wish," said Mom. "Then blow." Eleanor took a big breath. She blew hard. The flames went out. All four! Smoke curled up like little strings.

"Why did they go out?" asked Ben.

"Because I blew on them," said Eleanor. "Air makes the fire stop."

Then Grandpa rolled the cake to her on a little cart with one wobbly wheel. Eleanor cut the first slice. It was chocolate, her favorite.

"Look how strong I am," she said, lifting the big piece. "I am four now."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Leah held her doll tight. Mom said, "Let's find milk!" Leah loved the store. It was so big! She was so small.

First they went fast. The cart went zoom! Then they went slow. Slow by the apples, red and round. "Big apple," said Leah. She picked a small one too. "Small apple!" The small one fit in her hand.

Then they came to the cold door. Leah touched the glass. Brrr! It was cold in there. The milk felt cold, like ice, almost frozen. Then they walked past the bread. The oven was hot. Leah felt warm air on her face. "Hot!" she said.

Leah got one apple at snack time. She bit it. "Mom!" she whispered. "My small apple is all gone!" Mom smiled. "You ate it up, Leah." Leah hugged her doll. "More store tomorrow?"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Miles sat at the art table. He wanted to paint a green frog. He looked in the paint cup. There was red paint. There was blue paint. There was yellow paint. There was no green paint. "Oh no," said Miles.

A dog barked outside the window. Bark, bark. Miles looked up, then looked down again. He touched his own nose. He had a dot of yellow paint on his nose. He dipped his brush in yellow. Then he dipped it in blue. He stirred the paint round and round. The brush made him feel dizzy, so he stopped. The paint turned green. He stirred once more. Yellow and blue made green. "Yellow and blue make green," said Miles. He said it again. "Yellow and blue make green."

Miles painted a big green frog. The frog sat on a green leaf. His teacher walked by and smiled. "What a green frog," she said. Miles held up his brush. "I made the green myself," he said. The dog barked one more time outside. Bark, bark. Miles painted a little black dog next to his frog.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Xavier went to the grocery store with Mama. He reached for his soft bunny. Bunny was not in his pocket.

"Oh no," said Xavier. "Where is bunny?"

Mama smiled. "Think, Xavier. Where did you see bunny last?"

Xavier thought hard. "The lunch aisle! Bunny saw the bread."

They walked back to the lunch aisle. They looked by the bread. They looked by the apples. No bunny.

"Let us look again," said Mama.

They looked down low, near the floor. There was bunny! Bunny sat under the shelf, next to a big can of soup.

"Found you!" said Xavier. He hugged his soft bunny tight.

"Bunny likes soup," said Mama with a laugh.

"No, Mama," said Xavier. "Bunny fell down. The shelf is tall and bunny is small."

Mama laughed again. "You speak the truth, little one."

Xavier put bunny back in his pocket. He patted it two times. "Stay put, bunny. Stay put."

At home, they ate lunch together. Bunny sat on the table too, right next to the bread.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Kinsley went to Mia's house. Mia had a big doll named Baby Rose. "Baby Rose is crying," said Mia. The doll made a crying sound.

"We need to help her," said Kinsley. Mia made a bottle for the baby. Kinsley patted her back. But Baby Rose still cried. Kinsley looked all around. Then she saw it. The baby's blanket had fallen on the floor. She peeked under the small quilt top. The baby had no blanket on. "The baby is cold," said Kinsley. "She cries because she is cold."

Kinsley picked up the blanket. It had some lint on it. She helped clean it off with her hand. Then she tucked it around Baby Rose, right up to her chin. Mia turned off the crying sound. Baby Rose was quiet now. "She feels better," said Mia.

Then Mia brought a tiny pot and a tiny hat. "Baby Rose needs clothes for the cold day," she said. Kinsley put the hat on the baby's head. The play kitchen door was open, so Kinsley shut it. "Now the kitchen is warm too," she said. Mia smiled and rocked Baby Rose in her arms. "Time for sleep, baby," said Mia. Kinsley sang a little song, very soft. Baby Rose's eyes closed.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Julia stood on a small stool in the kitchen. She wanted warm milk in her cup. Mom was right there, making bread.

"The pot is hot," Mom said. "Wait a bit."

Julia touched the cold counter instead. Cold felt nice on her fingers. She looked at the big pot on the stove. Then she looked at her small cup. The big pot held lots of milk. Her small cup held just a little.

Mom poured the milk fast into the cup. It sloshed out! "Too fast makes a mess," Mom said. She wiped it up with a gray cloth. Then she poured again, slow and easy. This time not one drop fell.

Julia touched the side of the cup. "Still too hot," she said. Mom put the cup in cold water. The cold water took the heat away.

Julia touched it again. "Now it's just right!" She drank it all up.

Mom smiled. "You waited so well." Julia stood up tall and put her cup in the sink. Mom gave her a warm hug.

The gray cat walked in and rubbed Julia's back. Julia giggled. "The cat wants warm milk too," she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Nova sat at the little red table in art class. She wanted to paint a cow in green grass. But the green paint cup was empty. Nova looked and looked. No green anywhere.

Then she saw Sam by the shelf. Sam had a big cup of blue paint. "Can I have some blue?" Nova asked. Sam poured a little blue into her cup. "Thank you," said Nova. The teacher gave her a cup of yellow paint too, because Nova had asked so kindly.

Nova dipped her brush in blue. Then she dipped it in yellow. She stirred on her paper. The paint turned green! "Blue and yellow make green," Nova said out loud. She painted the grass high and high. Then she painted her cow standing in it. Sam leaned over to see. "Nice cow," he said. Nova smiled and painted one yellow flower too.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Charles went to book club with his mama. He wore his bear sweater. The sweater was itchy. He pulled his sleeve up and down.

The teacher held up a letter. "This is S," she said. Charles knew that one. "S goes sssss," he said, like a snake. All the kids laughed and hissed too. Ssss, ssss, ssss.

Then the teacher held up M. Charles did not know M. He frowned. Then he pressed his lips together and said, "Mmmmm." The letter looked like two bumps. It sounded like yum. "M is for my itchy sweater," Charles said. "Mmm, mmm, mmm!"

He tried B. "Buh, buh, buh," he said. "B is for bear!" He counted the letters he knew. One, S. Two, M. Three, B. Three letters!

His mama helped him take off the sweater. "Too itchy?" she asked. "Yes," said Charles. "But my ears are not itchy. My ears know three letters now." He patted his own ear and giggled.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Raphael ran into the doctor's office with his old toy truck. He could not wait!

A nurse said, "Time to check your eyes." Raphael looked with his eyes. He saw a big red E on the wall. Then the nurse said, "Now we check your ears." Raphael heard a beep with his ears. Beep! Beep!

The doctor came in. She said, "Smell this, taste this, touch this." Raphael smelled a sweet orange with his nose. He tasted a sour drop with his tongue. He touched a cold truck wheel with his fingers. "My eyes see, my ears hear, my nose smells, my tongue tastes, my fingers touch!" said Raphael. "Five things my body can do!"

The doctor laughed. "You got it!" Raphael drove his old truck all the way to the door. "My eyes see the door," he said. "Bye, truck! We come back soon!"

activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
story:
Kai stood in the garage with Dad. Dad played a song on his old radio. The song had a steady beat. Boom, boom, boom.

Kai wanted to sing along. But he did not know the words yet. He clapped too fast, like he was chasing the song. His claps ran ahead of the beat. "Too fast!" he laughed. His hands felt tired.

"Try one clap for each boom," said Dad. He tapped his foot. Boom, boom, boom. Kai watched Dad's foot. He waited for a tap. Then he clapped. Clap. Clap. Clap. "My claps go with the booms now!" said Kai. "The song goes slow, so I go slow."

Then Dad sang "Twinkle, Twinkle" two times. Kai listened with his ears and his eyes shut. On the third time, Kai opened his mouth. The words came out all by themselves. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star!" He sang the whole song from memory. Dad gave him a big hug. Kai felt warm like toast.

Then the radio stopped. The garage went quiet and still, like a frozen puddle. But Kai kept singing anyway. "How I wonder what you are!" Dad clapped the beat for him, boom, boom, boom, all the way to the end.

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
story:
Amelia looked out the window. Snow was on the grass. Snow was on her swing. No school today! It was a snow day at home.

Amelia ran to the back door. She opened it and stepped out. The snow felt cold on her hands. Her fingers hurt. She ran back inside. "Mommy, my hands are cold!"

Mommy gave her big red mittens. Mommy gave her a warm coat and a hat. "Now you can play," Mommy said.

Amelia went out again. This time her hands stayed warm. "The mittens keep my hands warm," she said. She patted the snow. She made a small snowball. Her hands were still warm!

A little bird sat on the fence. It looked cold. Amelia put some seeds on the snow. "Here, bird," she said. The bird flew down to eat.

From next door, she heard a loud sound. A train went by the houses. It sounded far away in the quiet snow. Amelia waved at it.

The snow looked pretty in the sun. It shone like sugar. Amelia made footprints all over the yard. Mommy called, "Cocoa time!"

Amelia ran inside. She held the warm cup with her mittens still on. "Warm hands, warm tummy," she said, and took a big sip.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Mateo jumped into the family car. "Where is Bunny?" he asked. Bunny was gone. "I want Bunny now!"

"Let's look," said Mama. Mateo peeked under the seat. He found a cookie. He found one shoe. No Bunny. "Bunny is not here," he said. "Bunny is all alone somewhere."

"Think," said Mama. "Where did you play with Bunny last?" Mateo scratched his hair. Then his eyes got big. "The toy store! I put Bunny on the shelf while we looked!" The shelf had lots of toys. Maybe Bunny was still there.

They drove fast, fast, fast. Mateo looked out the window the whole way. "Hurry, Mama, hurry!" he said. The store man smiled. "We do not sell bunnies like that," he said. "But we kept one safe for you." He held out Bunny!

Mateo hugged Bunny tight. "Bunny was on the shelf," he said. "That is where I left him!" He buckled Bunny in beside him. "You sit with me now," he said. "No more shelf for you, Bunny. Home we go!"

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Luke went to the mall with Dad. Luke was getting his first haircut. The chair was big and tall. Luke had to sit up high. Dad helped him climb in.

The hair lady put a cape on Luke. It snapped shut at his neck. Then she began to cut. Snip, snip, snip. Little bits of hair fell down. Luke looked at his lap. The hair did not touch his pants. Why not? He asked himself. The cape was the reason. The hair fell on the cape and slid off. "The hair slides down because the cape is smooth," Luke said out loud.

The hair lady put her scissors on the counter. There was a low shelf there. A magnet sat on the shelf. Her clips stuck to the magnet. They did not fall off. Luke watched them click together. "Can I bring one clip home?" Luke asked. "No, but you can hold it," she said.

Luke held the clip near the magnet. It jumped right onto it. The magnet pulled it fast. Luke laughed. Then Dad lifted him down. Luke looked in the mirror. His hair was short now. He touched his head with both hands. "Look, Dad, all gone!"

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Ava sat at the big table. There was a yellow pencil by her hand. Her teacher, Miss Kim, smiled. "Today we write our names," she said.

Ava grabbed the pencil in her whole fist. She pushed hard. The A came out fat and wobbly. It looked like a sleepy bee had walked across the paper. "Silly A," said Ava. Tom laughed next to her. "Mine looks like a snake," he said.

Miss Kim showed a trick. She put her thumb and one finger at the pencil tip. Then she tucked the pencil under her other fingers. Ava tried it. She pinched the tip, just like that. Her hand did not slip. She drew a straight line, then a line that leaned. "It's an A!" said Ava. She drew more. V. A. Again and again.

"Why is it easy now?" Tom asked. Ava held up the pencil. "Because my fingers lock it right here," she said. She pinched the tip tight and tapped it. "Now my letters can't run away."

Tom leaned over. "Can you write my name too?" Ava giggled. "T is easy. T is just a stick with a hat." She pressed her pencil down and began the first line.

activity: going to the dentist for the first time
story:
Harper held her mama's hand. The door said DENTIST. Harper did not want to go in.

A kind lady with gray hair smiled. "Hello, Harper," she said. "Come sit in my big chair."

The chair went up. The chair went back. Harper lay down like a sleepy mouse. "Why does the chair go back?" she asked.

"So I can see your teeth," the lady said. "Teeth hide in the back."

The lady held a little mirror. "Let's count your teeth," she said. "One, two, three." She touched each tooth softly. Harper counted too. "Four, five, six." They counted all the way to twenty.

Then the lady made the teeth clean. The brush was small and round. It tickled a little. Harper giggled.

The chair went up again. Harper looked in a mirror. Her teeth were shiny and white.

"I know why the chair goes back," Harper told Mama. "It goes back so the light can see my teeth. And the brush makes them clean."

"Twenty clean teeth," said the lady. "See you soon, Harper."

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Matteo went to the park with his bucket. He wanted to find five pretty things for Grandma.

His eyes saw a red leaf. He picked it up. His ears heard a bird sing. He listened and listened.

Then he found something soft. It was a fuzzy feather. He touched it with his fingers. His nose smelled something sweet. It came from a flower. He took one careful sniff. He put the flower in his bucket too.

"Four things," said Matteo. "I need one more."

His friend Mia came by. She held out a small berry. "Taste this," she said. "My mom says it is a sweet berry." Matteo tasted it with his tongue. It was sweet!

"Thank you, Mia," he said. "You helped me find five."

He counted his treasures. "My eyes, my ears, my fingers, my nose and my tongue helped me today. Five helpers for five things!"

He ran home with his bucket.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Levi got new blocks at school. He wanted to build a house for his toy animal. A big house, fast!

He stacked a circle block on the bottom. It rolled! The whole tower fell down. "Oh no!" said Levi. He tried again. The circle rolled again.

Then Levi saw a square block. It had flat sides. He put the square on the bottom. It did not roll. It stayed right there! Levi stacked a triangle on top for the roof. He used two rectangles for the walls. The tower stood tall.

"Look, teacher!" Levi called. "The square stays because it is flat. The circle rolls because it is round!" He put his animal inside the house. "You can stay here," he said. The animal fit just right.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Elizabeth went to the park with Grandma. She wanted to see the ducks. Grandma held her hand. "Stay close to me," said Grandma.

Elizabeth saw a big metal bench in the sun. She put her hand near it. The bench was very hot! She pulled her hand back fast. "Ouch," she said. The bench sat in the sun all morning. That was why it was hot. Grandma put her hand on the shady part. The shady part was cool. Elizabeth touched the shady part too. "Cool," she said.

Then Elizabeth saw something shiny by the path. It was a piece of broken glass. She wanted to touch it. But glass with sharp edges can cut. She did not touch it. She pointed and said, "Grandma, look!" Grandma picked it up with a gentle hand and put it in a bag. "Good looking, Elizabeth," said Grandma.

The ducks were by the pond. Elizabeth stayed right by Grandma. She dropped little crumbs one at a time. A duck came close and ate one. Elizabeth laughed. "The duck likes my crumbs," she said.

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
Thomas walked into the grocery store with his mom. It was cold outside, so he wore his red coat. But the coat was open, and Thomas felt chilly in the frozen food aisle.

"Try to zip it yourself," said Mom. Thomas pulled the zipper. It did not move. He pulled again. Still no zip. Thomas looked down. He saw the problem. His shirt was stuck in the zipper. The shirt was in the way, so the zipper could not close.

Thomas pulled the shirt out of the way. Then he pushed the little tab up, slowly. Zzzzzip! The coat closed all the way to his chin. "My shirt was in the line of the zipper," said Thomas. "Now it is not!"

"That is a neat zip," said Mom. Thomas smiled. At the checkout line, he unzipped his coat by himself too. Then he zipped it again, just to practice. "I can do it," said Thomas. "All by myself!"

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Jacob sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. He wanted to see Dr. Amy, but the door was closed. "Close your eyes," said Mom. Jacob closed them. Now he could not see the door at all. "My eyes make seeing work," said Jacob.

Dr. Amy came in. She had a picture of a river on her coat. Jacob saw the blue water. He heard her say hello with his ears. He touched her cold stethoscope with his fingers. Then Dr. Amy held up a jar. "Smell this," she said. Jacob's nose smelled oranges. He remembered oranges at Grandma's house.

At the end, Dr. Amy gave Jacob a little cup. His tongue tasted sweet juice. "Now my tummy will not feel weak," said Jacob. He held Mom's hand tight all the way home.
